stories.headline: Evening check: no reversal, but policy and litigation pressure widened further
stories.summary: The market view did not flip by evening. The most useful added signals are that the UK government backed away from an AI-training opt-out path after creative-industry backlash, and Google was pulled into music-training litigation over Lyria 3.

stories.headline: Google is now inside the music-training rights fight too
stories.summary: Billboard reported indie artists sued Google over alleged Lyria 3 training on unlicensed YouTube songs. This is an allegation rather than a legal finding, but it meaningfully weakens any assumption that large-platform distribution automatically means low rights risk.

stories.headline: The UK stepped back from a creator-hostile AI training default
stories.summary: Billboard reported the UK government no longer had a preferred opt-out approach after strong rejection from the creative industries. That suggests music-sector pressure can still shape public policy, not just courtroom outcomes.

stories.headline: BMG added another music-specific copyright front against Anthropic
stories.summary: Reuters reported BMG sued Anthropic over alleged use of copyrighted lyrics in Claude training, citing 493 infringed works and criticizing sourcing from unauthorized torrent sites. That keeps music-specific sourcing and substitution risk very live.

stories.headline: GEMA vs. Suno remains a concrete European test of output similarity and licensing
stories.summary: Music Business Worldwide reported the Munich hearing ended without a ruling and set a June 12 decision date. GEMA is pressing the argument that Suno outputs can be misleadingly similar to original songs in melody, harmony, and rhythm.

stories.headline: Google distribution and Suno product velocity still say the category is commercially real
stories.summary: Google is pushing Lyria 3 Pro into mainstream workflow surfaces, while MBW reported Suno launched v5.5 with voice capture and personal-style models. But those same moves also make identity control and rights posture more strategically important.

stories.headline: Musician adoption evidence still supports workflow-first products
stories.summary: Moises and Water & Music still show practical tools beating full-song generation in real usage. Stem separation led at 71%, versus 24% for full-song generation, while copyright and authenticity worries stayed high.

stories.headline: X remains more useful as a noise/weather check than a factual source
stories.summary: A small recent-search sample was again dominated by hobbyist AI-music publishing chatter, DSP release talk, ethics/copyright debate, and low-signal promotion. Directionally, that supports the view that AI music is leaking into mass self-publishing workflows and that trust-safe messaging is becoming part of the pitch.

themes.workflow_over_hype: The strongest evidence still favors AI tools that remove friction inside existing music workflows rather than tools that fully replace musicians.
themes.rights_cleanliness_matters_more: The legal and policy environment continues to reward clean sourcing, transparency, consent, and rights clarity.
themes.scale_is_real_but_not_enough: Google's distribution and Suno's scale/product pace show the category is real, but they also make generic AI music apps less defensible.
themes.trust_infrastructure_is_rising: Sony's deepfake takedowns, Deezer's detection licensing, STIM's licensing framework, the UK policy retreat, and Google litigation all point toward trust/compliance becoming product categories inside music tech.
themes.musio_implication: Musio should keep leaning toward trustworthy creator infrastructure: realistic musical output, human control, workflow fit, and commercially usable results.
